facts.statement: Utahraptor lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically from the Berriasian to the Valanginian stages, with a possible record extending into the Hauterivian–Barremian stages.

facts.statement: The genus Utahraptor was described in 1993 by James Kirkland and colleagues, with the type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi.
facts.quote: The genus was described in 1993 by American paleontologist James Kirkland and colleagues with the type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi

facts.statement: The fossils used to describe Utahraptor were originally unearthed from the Cedar Mountain Formation in Utah.
facts.quote: based on fossils that had been unearthed earlier from the Cedar Mountain Formation of Utah

facts.statement: Utahraptor is the largest known member of the family Dromaeosauridae, measuring approximately 6 to 7 meters in length and weighing around 500 kilograms.
facts.quote: It is the largest-known member of the family Dromaeosauridae, measuring about 6 - 7 m long and typically weighing around 500 kg

facts.statement: As a carnivore, Utahraptor was adapted to hunt animals such as ankylosaurs and iguanodonts within the Cedar Mountain Formation ecosystem.
facts.quote: Being a carnivore, Utahraptor was adapted to hunt the other animals of the Cedar Mountain Formation ecosystem such as ankylosaurs and iguanodonts

facts.statement: Evidence from leg physiology suggests Utahraptor was an ambush predator, contrasting with other dromaeosaurs that were pursuit predators.
facts.quote: Evidence from the leg physiology supports the idea of Utahraptor being an ambush predator, in contrast to other dromaeosaurs that were pursuit predators

facts.statement: The discovery of fossil remains of Utahraptor individuals of various ages together suggests the species was gregarious and practiced some form of post-nestling care.
facts.quote: Fossil remains of several individuals of various ages have been found together, suggesting that Utahraptor was gregarious (social) and practiced degrees of post nestling care

facts.statement: The first specimens of Utahraptor were found in 1975 by Jim Jensen in the Dalton Wells Quarry near Moab, Utah.
facts.quote: The first specimens of Utahraptor were found in 1975 by Jim Jensen in the Dalton Wells Quarry of Utah, near the town of Moab

facts.statement: Further remains of Utahraptor were uncovered in 1991 by James Kirkland, Robert Gaston, and Donald Burge in the Gaston Quarry in Grand County, Utah.
facts.quote: James Kirkland, Robert Gaston and Donald Burge uncovered further remains of Utahraptor in 1991 in the Gaston Quarry in Grand County, Utah

facts.statement: The type species Utahraptor ostrommaysi was named by Kirkland, Gaston, and Burge in June 1993.
facts.quote: The type species, Utahraptor ostrommaysi, was named by Kirkland, Gaston and Burge in June 1993

facts.statement: The genus name Utahraptor refers to Utah, the location where the remains were discovered.
facts.quote: The genus name Utahraptor is in reference to Utah, where the remains were found

facts.statement: The specific name ostrommaysi honors John Ostrom for his work on Deinonychus and Chris Mays for founding Dinamation and assisting in Utahraptor research.
facts.quote: The specific name, ostrommaysi, is in honor to John Ostrom for his investigations on Deinonychus and its relationships to birds, as well as Chris Mays, who helped in the research of Utahraptor by founding Dinamation

facts.statement: James Kirkland changed the species name from U. spielbergi to U. ostrommaysi shortly before publication due to threats of legal action from Universal Studios regarding the word "Jurassic" in museum exhibits.
facts.quote: Kirkland, however, later expressed that this was a misquote. He had changed the name to U. ostrommaysi shortly before the publication of the paper, as Universal Studios has begun threatening to sue museums that have exhibits with the word "Jurassic" in their titles

facts.statement: In 2000, George Olshevsky emended the specific name to the plural genitive ostrommaysorum.
facts.quote: In 2000, the specific name was emended by George Olshevsky to the plural genitive ostrommaysorum

facts.statement: In 2019, Costa and David criticized the emended name ostrommaysorum, arguing it lacks clear justification or explanation.
facts.quote: However, Thiago Vernaschi V. Costa and Normand David in 2019 criticized the use of the species name U. ostrommaysorum, since it has no clear justification or explanation

facts.statement: The characteristic "killing claw" of Utahraptor ostrommaysi may have measured approximately 24 centimeters in length.
facts.quote: The characteristic "killing claw" of dromaeosaurids may, in U. ostrommaysi, have measured about 24 cm in length

facts.statement: Utahraptor is classified as a genus of large dromaeosaurid dinosaur.
facts.quote: Utahraptor (meaning "Utah's predator") is a genus of large dromaeosaurid (a group of feathered carnivorous theropods) dinosaur

facts.statement: In 2019, Ruben Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi estimated that specimen BYUVP 15465 was 4.9 meters in length and weighed 280 kilograms.
facts.quote: Ruben Molina-Pérez and Asier Larramendi, in 2019, estimated that BYUVP 15465 was 4.9 m in length and weighed 280 kg

facts.statement: In 2013, Lindsay E. Zanno and Peter J. Makovicky estimated the body mass of Utahraptor at around 290 kilograms based on femoral length.
facts.quote: In 2013, based on femoral length, Lindsay E. Zanno and Peter J. Makovicky estimated its body mass at around 290 kg

facts.statement: Body mass estimates for specific specimens include 391 kg for BYUVP 2536, 481 kg for BYUVP 1833, and 777 kg for BYUVP 7510-18078.
facts.quote: The body masses of BYUVP 2536 and BYUVP 1833 were estimated around 391 and 481 kg, respectively, while BYUVP 7510-18078 was estimated to have weighed 777 kg

facts.statement: Researchers estimated in 1993 that the premaxilla of Utahraptor was approximately 250% larger than that of Deinonychus.
facts.quote: According to Kirkland and colleagues in 1993, the premaxilla of U. ostrommaysi was incredibly large compared to that of other dromaeosaurids, perhaps 250% larger than that of Deinonychus.

facts.statement: The tooth row of the Utahraptor premaxilla measured approximately 75 mm in length.
facts.quote: The alveolar process or tooth row of the premaxilla was around 75 mm in length.

facts.statement: The lower jaw of Utahraptor is known from several dentaries recovered from the Utahraptor Block.
facts.quote: The mandible (lower jaw) of U. ostrommaysi is known from several dentaries (the tooth-bearing portions at the front), recovered from the Utahraptor Block.

facts.statement: Teeth in the front of the Utahraptor lower jaw were procumbent, meaning they visibly protruded forward.
facts.quote: It indicates that the teeth of Utahraptor lower jaw were fairly procumbent anteriorly, meaning those towards the front would have visibly protruded forwards.

facts.statement: The second toe claw of the Utahraptor holotype measured 22 cm along its curve and is estimated to be 24 cm in total length.
facts.quote: The second pedal ungual, the bone on the second toe which would have supported this claw, is preserved in the holotype with a 22 cm length when measured along its outside curve, and is estimated to have measured 24 cm in total.

facts.statement: Shortened chevrons and prezygapophyses in the Utahraptor tail likely increased its flexibility compared to many other dromaeosaurs.
facts.quote: The chevrons and prezygapophyses of U. ostrommaysi tail appear to have been shortened, which would have increased the tail's overall flexibility in comparison to that of many other dromaeosaurs.

facts.statement: The size of flexor tubercles suggests Utahraptor had a strong grip on its feet, possibly stronger than Deinonychus relative to body size.
facts.quote: The size of the flexor tubercles on U. ostrommaysi pedal digits, to which digital flexors would have attached in life, suggests that it had a strong grip, perhaps more so than Deinonychus (which had smaller flexor tubercles) in proportion to body size.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the blade-like construction of Utahraptor hand claws might have been used to slash at prey.
facts.quote: However, they were more laterally compressed and were noted to have been more blade-like in construction, leading Kirkland and colleagues to suggest that U. ostrommaysi might have used them to slash at prey.

facts.statement: Researchers noted that Utahraptor was likely slower than Deinonychus and Velociraptor but faster than sauropods, with speeds similar to contemporary iguanodonts.
facts.quote: Kirkland and colleagues noted that given the large size of Utahraptor, it was not as fast as Deinonychus and Velociraptor; instead, it would have had a similar speed to the contemporary iguanodonts, though would have been faster than sauropods.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested Utahraptor could deliver kicks without losing balance, freeing its hands to dispatch prey, unlike lighter dromaeosaurids.
facts.quote: It was also suggested that lighter dromaeosaurids such as Velociraptor and Deinonychus relied on their hand claws to handle prey and retain balance while kicking it; in contrast to this, the heavily built Utahraptor may have been able to deliver kicks without the risk of losing balance, freeing the hands and using them to dispatch prey.

facts.statement: Utahraptor is classified as a member of the theropod family Dromaeosauridae, commonly known as raptors.
facts.quote: Utahraptor is a member of the family Dromaeosauridae, a clade of theropod dinosaurs commonly known as the "raptors".

facts.statement: Utahraptor is considered one of the largest, if not the largest, known representatives of the Dromaeosauridae family.
facts.quote: Utahraptor is one of the largest, if not the largest-known representative of the family.

facts.statement: James Kirkland and colleagues initially placed Utahraptor in the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae, which is now part of the clade Eudromaeosauria.
facts.quote: In their initial description of the genus, James Kirkland and colleagues placed Utahraptor within the subfamily Dromaeosaurinae, now part of the clade Eudromaeosauria.

facts.statement: A 2019 analysis suggested Utahraptor might belong to a clade outside Dromaeosaurinae, though it could be moved to Dromaeosaurinae or Velociraptorinae with minor changes.
facts.quote: An analysis in 2019 by Mickey Mortimer and colleagues recovered Achillobator, Deinonychus, Utahraptor and Yixiansaurus in a clade potentially outside of Dromaeosaurinae, though noted that it could be moved to either Dromaeosaurinae or Velociraptorinae in only two steps.

facts.statement: A nine-ton fossil block of sandstone containing Utahraptor bones was discovered in eastern Utah in 2001.
facts.quote: In 2001, Kirkland and colleagues pursued a graduate student's discovery of a bone protruding from a nine-ton fossil block of sandstone in eastern Utah.

facts.statement: Researchers speculate that the Utahraptor pack may have been mired in quicksand while attempting to scavenge carrion or attack helpless prey.
facts.quote: Kirkland speculated that the Utahraptor pack attempted to scavenge carrion or attack helpless prey mired in quicksand, and were themselves mired in the attempt to feed on the herbivore.

facts.statement: It is unclear whether all Utahraptor individuals in the fossil block were mired simultaneously or were drawn in one by one.
facts.quote: Whether all the Utahraptor individuals were mired simultaneously or were drawn in, one-by-one is unclear.

facts.statement: Further examination suggests the number of Utahraptor remains in the block may be double the previously assumed amount.
facts.quote: Further examination of the block suggests that the number of Utahraptor remains may be double the amount previously assumed.

facts.statement: The discovery of Utahraptor in a mud trap implies the species exhibited post-nestling care and gregarious behavior.
facts.quote: Additionally, the discovery of Utahraptor in the mud-trap implies it exhibited a degree of post-nestling care and gregariousness.

facts.statement: Utahraptor lived in the lower part of the Cedar Mountain Formation, specifically the Yellow Cat Member.
facts.quote: Utahraptor lived in the lower part of the Cedar Mountain Formation, a bed known as the Yellow Cat Member.

facts.statement: Thomas R. Holtz estimated that Utahraptor existed between 130 and 125 million years ago.
facts.quote: The paleontologist Thomas R. Holtz estimated that Utahraptor existed between 130 million and 125 million years ago.

facts.statement: Joeckel and colleagues (2019) used radiometric and palynological dating to conclude the Yellow Cat Member is older than previous estimations.
facts.quote: Using advanced methods of radiometric and palynological dating, Joeckel and colleagues (2019) concluded that the Yellow Cat Member is indeed older than previous estimations.

facts.statement: Deposition of the Yellow Cat Member occurred between 139 ± 1.3 and 134.6 ± 1.7 million years ago, corresponding to Berriasian to Late Valanginian stages.
facts.quote: The deposition occurred between 139 ± 1.3 million to 134.6 ± 1.7 million years ago, or, Berriasian to Late Valanginian stages.

facts.statement: Utahraptor fossils are currently known only from the upper Yellow Cat Member.
facts.quote: Utahraptor fossils are only currently known within the upper Yellow Cat Member.

facts.statement: Utahraptor was a major carnivore in the Early Cretaceous Arches region and could likely attack prey larger than itself.
facts.quote: Utahraptor had an important ecological role as a major carnivore of the paleofauna of the present-day Arches region during the Early Cretaceous, and could probably attack prey larger than itself.

facts.statement: If proven, group hunting by Utahraptors measuring at least 3.5 meters and weighing 70 kg could have killed prey up to 8 meters long and weighing 1 to 2 tons.
facts.quote: Group hunting of individuals of at least 3.5 m and 70 kg, if proven, could have killed 8 m prey of a weight of 1 to 2 t.

facts.statement: Sauropods ranging around 20 meters in length may have been an important part of the Utahraptor diet.
facts.quote: Additionally, sauropods ranging around 20 m may have been an important part of its diet.

facts.statement: Contemporaneous paleofauna in the upper Yellow Cat Member included iguanodonts like Hippodraco and Cedrorestes, theropods like Martharaptor and Nedcolbertia, the nodosaurid Gastonia, and sauropods Cedarosaurus and Moabosaurus.
facts.quote: Paleofauna that were contemporaneous with the dromaeosaurid in the upper Yellow Cat Member included numerous dinosaurs, such as the medium-sized iguanodonts Hippodraco and Cedrorestes, the smaller theropods Martharaptor and Nedcolbertia, the nodosaurid Gastonia, and the sauropods Cedarosaurus and Moabosaurus.

facts.statement: Cifelliodon is the only known mammal from the Upper Yellow Cat Member.
facts.quote: The only known mammal from the Upper Yellow Cat Member is Cifelliodon.

facts.statement: In 2018, a 10-year-old student named Kenyon Roberts proposed that Utahraptor be the Utah state dinosaur, a proposal approved by the Senate.
facts.quote: In 2018, it was proposed by a 10-year-old elementary school student, Kenyon Roberts, that Utahraptor be the Utah state dinosaur, an act that was approved by the Senate.

facts.statement: In 2021, Steve Eliason proposed Utahraptor State Park at the discovery site, a proposal by student Kenyon Roberts that was approved by the state House.
